Newborn Care

CHARGE syndrome: diagnosis, health care and communication support

Updated: October 19, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

CHARGE syndrome can affect several body systems from birth, but no two children have the same combination of needs. Recognising the pattern helps the team protect breathing, feeding, hearing and vision while planning development and family support. A diagnosis should lead to an individual care plan, not a prediction that a child will have every listed difficulty.

What the name means, and what it cannot predict

The letters CHARGE refer to coloboma, heart differences, choanal atresia, growth and developmental differences, genital development and ear differences. Coloboma means that part of an eye structure did not form; choanal atresia means a blockage at the back of the nose. This is a memory aid for a pattern, not a requirement to have all six features. The condition is rare, and estimates depend on how cases are identified rather than one exact worldwide rate.

The wider pattern can include cranial-nerve differences, cleft lip or palate, problems swallowing, a soft or unstable airway, kidney differences and hormone problems. Some needs are obvious in a newborn, while others emerge with growth. Hearing or sight may be mildly or substantially affected; neither complete deafness nor blindness is inevitable. Facial shape or a palm crease alone cannot diagnose the syndrome or establish a child’s learning potential.

CHD7, clinical diagnosis and family questions

Many cases involve a disease-causing change in CHD7, a gene involved in regulating other genes during development. Most such changes are new in the child, although inheritance from a parent and parental mosaicism can occur. A child’s condition is not evidence that a parent caused it. A genetics professional can explain parental testing and future-pregnancy options; absence of family history does not mean recurrence is impossible, and severity can differ within a family.

CHD7-related disorder covers a wider spectrum than clinical CHARGE syndrome, so finding a pathogenic variant does not automatically mean the full syndrome. Conversely, a negative test does not alone rule out clinical CHARGE. The team combines the pattern of findings with appropriate genetic testing; additional deletion/duplication analysis, a broader gene panel or genomic testing may be considered. A variant of uncertain significance is not a confirmed diagnosis. Ask what the result establishes, what remains uncertain and whether later reassessment could help.

Eyes, ears, balance and cranial nerves

Coloboma can affect the iris, retina, optic nerve or another part of one or both eyes. Its location and extent matter for sight; some children also have small or underdeveloped eyes. A specialist eye examination, including examination of the back of the eye, helps plan glasses, low-vision support and any treatment for associated problems. Facial weakness can make complete eyelid closure difficult, so eye protection may need a specific plan. Treatment cannot simply replace missing eye tissue.

Outer, middle and inner ear differences can cause conductive, sensorineural or mixed hearing loss. Inner-ear balance structures may also affect head control, walking and how visual information is used. Cranial nerves can affect smell, facial movement, hearing and the coordination of sucking and swallowing. Arrange audiology even after a reassuring newborn screen, with ENT, vision and movement specialists as needed. Hearing aids or implants are individual options; anatomy, nerve function and goals must be assessed rather than assuming every device will work.

Breathing, swallowing and early feeding care

Nasal passages may be narrow or blocked on one or both sides. Cleft palate, laryngomalacia or tracheomalacia, where parts of the airway are unusually floppy, and other airway differences can add problems. Some children have oesophageal atresia, an interrupted food pipe, or a tracheoesophageal fistula, an abnormal connection to the windpipe, including H-type fistula without interruption. Airway and paediatric surgical teams decide what support or repair is needed; a known diagnosis does not make new breathing trouble safe to watch at home.

Swallowing difficulties can let milk, food or saliva enter the airway. Coughing or choking during feeds, a wet or gurgly voice, long feeds, repeated chest infections or poor weight gain deserve assessment. A feeding and swallowing team may use selected swallow studies and plan texture, positioning, nutrition or tube support for that child. Reflux and gut-movement problems can also need treatment. Do not force a feed, thicken liquids or adjust a feeding or airway tube without the team’s instructions; breathing distress during feeding needs immediate help.

Heart, kidneys, growth and hormones

Heart findings range from smaller structural differences to complex defects; rhythm or blood-vessel problems may also matter. Kidney or urinary-tract differences can include a small or missing kidney, reflux of urine or drainage problems. Cardiac assessment and renal ultrasound help identify needs that may not be obvious from appearance. A small chin, facial asymmetry, characteristic ears or an unusual palm crease can contribute to the overall assessment but are not a home diagnostic checklist.

Growth may slow because of feeding difficulty, illness or hormone problems; short stature does not automatically mean growth-hormone deficiency. Thyroid and growth assessment are tailored to the child. Reduced hormone signalling can affect genital development and delay, interrupt or prevent puberty in any sex. Undescended testes, a small penis or differences in reproductive structures may need assessment, but genital appearance does not identify every hormone problem. Endocrinology can plan tests, puberty treatment and bone-health care when indicated; growth or sex hormones are not universal treatments to start independently.

A coordinated assessment rather than one decisive sign

A paediatrician and clinical genetics team usually coordinate the diagnosis with other specialists. The plan may include eye examination, hearing and balance assessment, ENT airway review, heart tests such as an ECG and echocardiogram, kidney imaging, growth and hormone assessment, and feeding and developmental evaluation. Symptoms can also lead to assessment for seizures, spine problems, immune difficulties or other findings. Imaging and additional tests should answer a clinical question; not every child needs the same scans or sedation.

Ask who holds the complete care plan and how results will reach the family and other clinicians. The team should explain alternative conditions with overlapping signs and the limits of any genetic result. Assessments of movement, learning and communication must be accessible to the child’s hearing, vision and physical needs. Limited speech, delayed responses or a difficult test session should not be treated as proof of a fixed intellectual limit. Do not wait for every diagnostic question to be resolved before arranging needed sensory and developmental support.

Treatment targets the child’s actual needs

There is no single treatment that removes the underlying syndrome, but many specific problems can be treated or supported. Early priorities may be a safe airway, heart treatment, repair of an oesophageal or palatal difference, and adequate nutrition. Later care can include eye and hearing support, feeding therapy, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, dental care and selected endocrine, kidney or other treatment. Timing, benefits and risks depend on the findings, age and family goals, not on completing every intervention on a list.

Tell every surgical, dental and anaesthesia team about airway, swallowing, heart and previous anaesthetic problems, as well as communication needs. CHARGE can increase airway and recovery risks around anaesthesia. Specialists may coordinate necessary procedures and plan extra observation when appropriate; this does not mean avoiding needed treatment or combining all procedures regardless of risk. Ask for a written plan for pain relief, feeding, equipment and recovery. Do not change medicines or attempt procedures based on a general syndrome description.

Communication, learning and behaviour deserve accessible support

Development is influenced by hearing, vision, balance, health, opportunities and individual learning needs. Early speech-language, sensory, movement and educational support can build access to play and participation. A communication plan may combine usable speech and sound, gesture, sign, pictures, meaningful objects, touch cues or assistive technology. The best combination depends on the child; speech should not be the only accepted way to communicate, and combined sensory loss needs specialist assessment rather than an assumption of no ability.

Give the child time to respond, offer meaningful choices and use predictable routines in a safe, comfortable setting. Notice subtle attempts to communicate and share what works between home and school. New distress or a change in behaviour may signal pain, poor sleep, sensory overload, anxiety or a communication barrier. Some people also need mental-health or neurodevelopmental assessment. Repetitive behaviours or obsessive-compulsive symptoms can occur, but they are not a fixed personality or an inevitable diagnosis at a particular age. Support should seek the cause of difficulty and respect the person’s preferences.

Family priorities and follow-up across the lifespan

Families know their child’s interests, communication and day-to-day changes. Ask the team to agree on priorities that are workable at home, rather than presenting every possible problem at once. Shared accessible play, appropriate positioning and opportunities to explore can support participation; equipment and activities should fit the child’s sensory and physical needs. Early-intervention services, school accommodations, specialist deafblind services where relevant, family networks and respite or social-work support can all have a role.

Keep an updated summary of diagnoses, medicines, feeding and airway instructions, communication methods and emergency contacts. Regular reviews should follow sight, hearing, nutrition, growth, sleep, development, dental health and any established organ problems. Puberty, bone health, independence and transition to adult care need planning too. New feeding, hearing, vision or balance concerns deserve review between appointments. Outlook varies widely; neither an early severe illness nor a mild relative’s experience gives a certain forecast for another person.

When to seek urgent or emergency help

Get emergency help immediately for difficulty or pauses in breathing, blue or grey colour, unusual pallor or mottling with illness, choking with ineffective breathing, fainting or loss of consciousness, difficulty waking, a seizure or a non-fading rash. A baby under three months with a temperature of 38°C or higher, or a baby with a temperature below 36°C, needs immediate hospital assessment. Do not continue feeding a baby who is struggling to breathe or wait for several signs together. Use the child’s emergency plan and local emergency services; a familiar diagnosis is not a reason to delay.

Seek prompt clinical advice for new or worsening feed-related coughing or choking, poor intake, repeated vomiting, fewer wet nappies, fever or signs of infection, pain or a marked change in usual behaviour. Follow any stricter instructions from the specialist team. New flashes, floaters, a shadow or curtain in vision, or suddenly blurred vision need urgent eye assessment, not the next routine appointment. Young children may show a change in visual behaviour rather than describe it. Ask the team how to recognise and act on changes for your child.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask which findings need treatment now, which need surveillance, and who coordinates the complete genetic, sensory and organ-care plan.

Get individual feeding, airway, medicine and procedure instructions in writing; tell every anaesthesia team about the child’s health and communication needs.

Agree on accessible communication and learning support with the child, family and school, and keep a practical emergency-contact and follow-up plan.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organise specialist appointments, feeding and sleep observations, prescribed medicines, communication preferences and questions about pending tests. It cannot diagnose CHARGE, interpret a CHD7 result, assess safe swallowing or breathing, or replace urgent care. Follow the child’s clinical and accessibility plans even when an app record appears reassuring.

When to seek help

Breathing difficulty or pauses, blue or grey colour, choking with ineffective breathing, fainting or loss of consciousness, difficulty waking, a seizure or a non-fading rash require immediate emergency help. A baby under three months at 38°C or higher, or a baby below 36°C, needs immediate hospital assessment. Do not trial feeds during respiratory distress or manipulate airway or feeding equipment yourself. Seek prompt advice for new feeding problems, illness, pain or changed behaviour, and urgent eye assessment for new flashes, floaters, a curtain or sudden blur. Use the specialist emergency plan without waiting for routine review.

Evidence notes updated: October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

  • CHARGE is a variable multisystem pattern; not every child has every feature or complete hearing and sight loss.
  • Clinical assessment and genetic interpretation work together; a CHD7 uncertain variant or negative result cannot settle every question.
  • Breathing, swallowing, heart health and nutrition may need early coordinated care, followed by lifelong individual review.
  • Hearing, vision, balance and communication support should start early and reflect each child’s strengths and preferences.
  • Use a clear family care and emergency plan; new symptoms must not be dismissed as simply part of the syndrome.

Frequently asked questions

What causes CHARGE syndrome?

Many cases involve a disease-causing CHD7 change, usually new in the child, but inherited variants and parental mosaicism can occur. Genetic counselling explains the actual result and family risk. It is not evidence that a parent caused the condition, and recurrence is not automatically impossible.

Which signs can occur?

Possible findings include coloboma, ear and hearing or balance differences, blocked nasal passages, cranial-nerve effects on smell, facial movement or swallowing, heart and kidney differences, cleft palate, growth or hormone problems and an oesophageal or airway connection. The combination and severity vary; a list cannot diagnose one child.

Does every child have an identifiable CHD7 variant?

Not finding a CHD7 variant does not by itself rule out clinical CHARGE. Tests have different limits, and further testing or reassessment may be useful. A pathogenic CHD7 finding also covers a broader spectrum than full clinical CHARGE. A variant of uncertain significance is not a confirmed diagnosis.

Can CHARGE be treated?

Specific problems can be treated even though there is no single cure for the whole syndrome. Care may involve airway, heart or feeding treatment, selected operations, sensory support, therapies and endocrine or other care. The plan is based on the individual, not a standard list of treatments for everyone.

Does the diagnosis mean blindness, deafness or a fixed learning limit?

No. Vision, hearing and learning needs vary. Coloboma does not always remove all sight. Communication and cognitive assessment need to account for sensory and physical access; limited speech is not proof of a fixed intellectual limit. Early support can use multiple communication methods.

Why are growth and puberty checked?

Feeding, illness and hormone problems can affect growth. Growth-hormone deficiency is only one possible explanation. Hormone signalling may also delay or interrupt puberty, sometimes without obvious genital differences at birth. An endocrinologist decides appropriate tests and any treatment.

How can families support communication?

Ask for an individual plan using the child’s available senses and preferred methods, such as speech, sign, gesture, meaningful objects, pictures, touch cues or technology. Allow response time, offer choices and share consistent approaches across home and school. Check pain, sleep and access barriers when behaviour changes.

What should not wait for a routine appointment?

Breathing difficulty or pauses, blue or grey colour, choking without effective breathing, fainting or loss of consciousness, difficulty waking, a seizure or a non-fading rash need emergency help. A baby under three months with at least 38°C or a baby below 36°C needs immediate hospital assessment. New feeding difficulties, illness or marked behaviour changes need prompt advice. New flashes, floaters, a visual curtain or sudden blur need urgent eye assessment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
